quote: Remark 3.1. On using Theorem 3.1(ii), one can easily find out a lower bound for the reliability function of the largest claims having heterogeneous portfolios of risks in the form of reliability of the largest claims having homogeneous portfolio of risks. Consider a T-transform matrix T_{0.5} of order 2 x 2, where the first and second rows are same and equal to (1/2, 1/2). Let (psi(p1), psi(p2)) = (e^{-p1}, e^{-p2}) and 1/theta = (1/theta_1, 1/theta_2). Further, assume (psi(q1), psi(q2)) = ((e^{-p1} + e^{-p2})/2, (e^{-p1} + e^{-p2})/2) and (1/delta_1, 1/delta_2) = ((theta_1+theta_2)/(2 theta_1 theta_2), (theta_1+theta_2)/(2 theta_1 theta_2)). ... by Theorem 3.1(ii), we can propose a lower bound of the reliability function of U_{2:2} as F_bar_{2:2}(t) >= [1 - {1 + ln((e^{-p1}+e^{-p2})/2)} {1 - F^alpha((t - lambda)(theta_1+theta_2)/(2 theta_1 theta_2))}]^2.

quote: Counterexample 3.1. Let F(t) = 1 - (1 + t/5)^{-4}, t > 0 and psi(p) = 1 - p^3. It is easy to check that psi(p) is decreasing and concave. So, the condition in (C10) is relaxed. Let us take (alpha_1, alpha_2) = (beta_1, beta_2) = (0.01, 0.01), (1/theta_1, 1/theta_2) = (0.7, 0.6), (1/delta_1, 1/delta_2) = (0.66, 0.64), (lambda_1, lambda_2) = (mu_1, mu_2) = (0.9, 0.9), (p_1, p_2) = ((0.2)^{1/3}, (0.5)^{1/3}) and (q_1, q_2) = ((0.32)^{1/3}, (0.38)^{1/3}). Consider a T-transform matrix T_{0.6} = ((0.6, 0.4),(0.4, 0.6)). It can be shown that (psi(q_1), psi(q_2); 1/delta_1, 1/delta_2) = (psi(p_1), psi(p_2); 1/theta_1, 1/theta_2) T_{0.6}, which produces chain majorization. Further, the matrix is in M_2. Based on this present setup, we have F_{2:2}(1.5) - G_{2:2}(1.5) = 1.5928 x 10^{-5} (> 0) and F_{2:2}(1.6) - G_{2:2}(1.6) = -1.9324 x 10^{-4} (< 0). ... It establishes that Theorem 3.1(ii) does not hold, if (C10) is taken out.

quote: Counterexample 3.2. Consider the same baseline distribution function as in Counterexample 3.1. Suppose psi(p) = - ln p. Here, one can check that (C1) and (C10) are satisfied. Set (alpha_1, alpha_2) = (beta_1, beta_2) = (0.01, 0.01), (1/theta_1, 1/theta_2) = (0.5, 0.3), (1/delta_1, 1/delta_2) = (0.32, 0.48), (lambda_1, lambda_2) = (mu_1, mu_2) = (0.9, 0.9), (psi(p_1), psi(p_2)) = (0.23, 0.69) and (psi(q_1), psi(q_2)) = (0.644, 0.276). For a T-transform matrix T_{0.1} = ((0.1, 0.9),(0.9, 0.1)), we have (psi(q); 1/delta) = (psi(p); 1/theta) T_{0.1}. Thus, from Definition 2.4, chain majorization holds. Again, (psi(p); 1/theta) does not belong to M_2. Now, considering the assumed numerical values, we get F_{2:2}(1.6) - G_{2:2}(1.6) = -9.2138 x 10^{-6} (< 0) and F_{2:2}(1.7) - G_{2:2}(1.7) = 5.0560 x 10^{-5} (> 0), which negates the usual stochastic order, stated in Theorem 3.1(ii).

quote: Counterexample 3.3. Consider the baseline distribution function as F(t) = 1 - (1 + 5t)^{-1/5}, t > 0, for which the hazard rate function r(x) is decreasing and convex. Let psi(p) = 1 - p^2. Clearly, psi(p) does not satisfy (C9). Set (alpha_1, alpha_2) = (beta_1, beta_2) = (1, 1), (theta_1, theta_2) = (delta_1, delta_2) = (sqrt(0.5), sqrt(0.5)), (lambda_1, lambda_2) = (0.9, 0.6), (mu_1, mu_2) = (0.81, 0.69), (p_1, p_2) = (sqrt(0.2), sqrt(0.3)) and (q_1, q_2) = (sqrt(0.23), sqrt(0.27)). Consider a T-transform matrix T_{0.7} = ((0.7, 0.3),(0.3, 0.7)). It can be shown that (mu; psi(q)) = (lambda; psi(p)) T_{0.7}, which yields chain majorization. Further, (lambda; psi(p)) in M_2. Denote eta(t) = r~_{2:2}(t) - s~_{2:2}(t). Then, eta(1.7) = 1.3522 x 10^{-4} (> 0) and eta(1.8) = -2.0998 x 10^{-4} (< 0), which shows that eta(t) changes sign, when t travels from 0 to infinity. Graph is presented in Figure 2(a) for clear view. Thus, U_{2:2} is not rh-ordered with V_{2:2}.

quote: Example 5.2. Let {X1, X2} and {Y1, Y2} be two collections of independent random variables such that Xi ~ F^alpha((x - lambda_i)/theta) and Yi ~ F^alpha((x - mu_i)/theta), for i = 1, 2. Set the baseline distribution function as Marshall-Olkin extended quasi Lindley distribution. ... Consider lambda = (5, 6.1), mu = (5.44, 5.66), theta = 0.01, alpha = 0.52, psi(p) = (0.2, 0.5), psi(q) = (0.32, 0.38). Here, psi(p) = p^2, which is increasing and convex with respect to p. Let T_{0.6} = ((0.6, 0.4),(0.4, 0.6)). Then, (psi(p1), psi(p2); lambda1, lambda2) >> (psi(q1), psi(q2); mu1, mu2). Thus, as an application of Corollary 5.3, we have U_{2:2} >=st V_{2:2}. The graph of F_{2:2}(t) - G_{2:2}(t) is given in Figure 3(a), that verifies Corollary 5.3.
